chapter_theme: The first half of the marutham section: the wife refusing the bard who comes as the straying man's go-between (124 to 127, 131 to 133, 136), mocking his lute, his modes and his lies; the man's field town, its paddy and lotus likened to a dancing or bathing woman's jewels, as the place she will not enter (128, 129); her doubt at his return (134) and wonder at his servitude to another woman (135); and the field town described as the father's town of a little boy with a toy chariot (124, 125, 137 to 139).

124.reading: The wife tells the bard of the sevvazhi lute that, before his little son could even appear drawing his fine toy chariot along this way by hand, the lord of the town of fine fields had bathed in this stream, embraced the shoulders of her 'younger sisters', and grown keener for them after.
124.nuance: The son with his toy chariot is used as a clock: the man went to the other women 'before the boy appears', so the claim the child should make on him came too late. எங்கையர், 'my younger sisters', is the wife's barbed name for the other women.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's embrace of other women, the marutham situation of straying

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the vocative பாண்மகனே; the colophon gives no thurai; she refuses the bard who comes for the man

125.reading: The wife asks the bard of the great-stemmed lute to tell her whether, before the little mahout of a clay elephant comes out with his drum on its hanging stick, the man will pass her guarded door and go off to the quarter of the women with hanging bangles.
125.nuance: Like 124, the poem sets the man's going against the boy at play: the child is a mahout of a clay elephant, his drum a toy, a parody of the royal procession the father might be leading instead.

thinai_evidence.note: the quarter of the bangled women he goes to

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the vocative; the colophon gives no thurai

126.reading: The wife tells the bard of the vilari lute not to call for her in vain; instead, stirring his strings, he should go and say it over there, where it will be heard, before the lord of the flowering fields enters his new house.
126.nuance: விளரி is the mode of lament: she names the bard by the tune of grief even as she sends him back to the house of pleasure.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's 'new house', the other woman's

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the vocative; the colophon gives no thurai; she refuses the bard

127.reading: The wife says the bard rose and left without telling them the truth about the lord of the town of soft, noisy fields, who does not come near this house, pleading his family's standing, and bids him go announce it instead to the adorned women he joins so eagerly.

thinai_evidence.note: the adorned women the man joins

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the bard is addressed in the second person (எழுந்துபோய்); the colophon gives no thurai

128.reading: Of the lord of the fields where red paddy stands up to touch the red lotus and looks like the forehead jewel of a woman who leaps into the stream to bathe, the speaker says that to love his friendship and then hold apart and bear the pain is the better course.
128.nuance: The vehicle of the simile is the ornament of a woman bathing in the stream, so the other woman (punal aadal was the man's sport with her) is set inside the description of his own fields. Close in frame to 129.

thinai_evidence.note: the fields and the water-sport of the marutham man

comparisons.tenor: the red paddy ear standing against the red lotus

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon gives no thurai

129.reading: The lord of the famed fields, where ears of red paddy bowing over unwithering lotuses look like the brow ornament of a dancer dancing in an undanced hall: better not to enter his good house.
129.nuance: As in 128 the comparison borrows a dancing woman's ornament for the field, so the man's landscape is already furnished with the women of his straying; the speaker answers it by refusing his 'good house' (நல்லகம்), an ironic name.

thinai_evidence.note: the field town and the refusal of his house

comparisons.tenor: the paddy ears bowing over the lotus, likened to a dancing woman's brow ornament

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon gives no thurai

130.reading: The wife says that the bards who sing the man's praise turned to blaming those who stood by her at the very time she took for truth the false coaxing of the lord of the full-watered town, who has no true tenderness.
130.nuance: The pair மெய்ம்மருட்டு / பொய்ம்மருட்டு sets a true beguiling, which the man is not capable of, against the false one she received.

thinai_evidence.note: the false coaxing of the marutham man

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon gives no thurai; the addressee is uncertain

131.reading: The wife tells the bard, whose lute is curved like a bent prawn and who has no good nature, that he need not fashion words to open a reconciliation: she was roused for good on the day she heard the lies of the lord of the flowered pond, where bent prawns look like strung bows.
131.nuance: The two similes are chained: the bard's lute is like the prawn, and the prawn of the man's pond is like a strung bow, so the instrument that comes to make peace is lined up with a weapon drawn. The bard's lute and the man's lie (பொய், inside பொய்கை) meet in one line.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's lies and the pond of his field town

comparisons.tenor: the bent prawns of the man's pond

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the vocative பாண; the colophon gives no thurai; she refuses the bard

132.reading: The wife tells the bard he was confused in thinking the man was among other women when he is among her own 'younger sisters', and that, going from here without a word, each of his evenings ends among the newer women.
132.nuance: The bard's excuse is turned against him: whether the women are 'others' or her 'sisters', the man is with them.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the vocative பாண; the colophon gives no thurai

133.reading: The wife asks the bard of the paalai lute whether he does not, as before, play the evening mode to soothe his master; he does not know where the morning mode should be played, and since he has bound himself to lies, let him find out the place where she wastes away.
133.nuance: The modes are named by their hours (paalai, evening, morning): the bard plays the evening to the man at the other house and does not know the morning, the hour of the wife's house, so his music itself keeps the man's timetable.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard serving the straying man with lies

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the vocative; the colophon gives no thurai

134.reading: The speaker wonders whether it is because the bond of the great does not decay, or because they look to the worth of old intimacy, that she, a humble servant who never asked, received the grace that the many the master of the house has taken did not.
134.nuance: The two words of the Kural's chapter on old friendship, கிழமை and பழமை, are set as alternatives: was his return a matter of character or of looking to old use? The question (கொல்லோ ... கொல்லோ) leaves it open, and அடியேன் may be humble or bitter.

thinai_evidence.note: the master of the house who has taken many women

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon gives no thurai; she seems to receive the man back, the addressee is a guess

135.reading: The speaker tells her friend that in all she has heard and seen on earth and in heaven she never knew such an end: she heard later that, while her own ornaments slipped away, he bowed low before the woman who torments him, never failing in his service.

thinai_evidence.note: the man bowing to another woman

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the vocative ஏழாய்; the colophon gives no thurai

136.reading: The wife tells the bard she will rise and go the way her 'sisters' do, since the man, not knowing that his own young one is living here, ran there distractedly, and his straying has grown and grown.

thinai_evidence.note: the man running to other women

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the vocative; the colophon gives no thurai

137.reading: A black-horned, red-eyed buffalo of the fields tramples the soft, thick-jointed sugarcane, tangles the water lilies with its fierce horns, and, having fed its fill, sinks down with its tethers swaying.
137.nuance: Near miss for ullurai: the buffalo trampling the cane and tangling the lilies maps readily onto the straying man (two pairs can be named), but neither the poem nor the colophon states the situation, so condition 4 fails and the buffalo stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo, cane and lilies of the watered fields

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the poem gives only the scene and the colophon no thurai; read with 138 and 139, it opens the description of the boy's father's town

iraicchi.act: the mother beast, thinking of her calf, lets her milk run
iraicchi.sense: even the cattle of his own town yearn toward their young, yet the father of this boy stays away from him

138.reading: In the town of this boy's father, the milk a buffalo lets fall as she thinks of her calf, pressed out by her feet, splashes hard on the lotus and sets the swan crying, so that whoever goes there and looks comes back exclaiming in wonder.
138.nuance: The man is named only as 'this boy's father', and the town's richness is a mother's milk running for an absent calf.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife naming the man only as the boy's father, in a field town

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; she speaks of the boy (இவன்) to an unnamed hearer; the colophon gives no thurai

139.reading: In the shade where marutham and kaanji trees rise together, with the din of men toiling behind their oxen and herons picking among the cool fields, lies the town of the father of the boy whose chariot does not run.
139.nuance: ஊராத்தேரான், 'the one with the chariot that does not run', names the child by his toy, and the man only through the child: the town is his father's, not her husband's.

thinai_evidence.note: the marutham tree and the watered fields

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; with 138 she describes the father's town in the boy's presence; the colophon gives no thurai

links.note: Ainkurunuru 66: the wife asks who the woman is who snatched away his coming home to his rich house when he was thinking of his toddling son with his little chariot (தேரொடு தளர்நடைப் புதல்வனை). Thinaimalai 124: before the boy appears drawing his toy chariot this way, the man has already bathed and embraced her 'sisters'.
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru 66 grants that the toddler with his chariot did pull the father toward home and blames a rival for stopping him, while the venba times the man's straying 'before the boy appears' and so denies the child ever had that pull, which shows the toy-chariot son working as the conventional test of a straying father's heart, passed in one poem and failed in the other.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 403: watching the boy, who bears his grandfather's name, pull his little chariot with tottering steps, the man's heart grows great toward the son as well as the wife. Thinaimalai 139: the wife names the field town only as the town of the father of the boy whose chariot does not run (ஊராத்தேரான் தந்தை). On the reading that 139 speaks during the man's absence, the two claim opposite effects for the same sight.
links.teaches: In the mullai poem the son's toy chariot binds the father to the house, while the marutham wife uses the same child to name a man who is not there, so the pair shows the son as the household's strongest tie and, when that tie fails, the wife's way of addressing the father without speaking to him.

links.note: Kalittokai 81: the boy moves his toy chariot by hand in the yard (கால் வல் தேர் கையின் இயக்க), the father is caught coming from another woman, and the wife ends by going to the boy like a cow to the place where its calf is tied (கன்று யாத்த உழிச் செல்லும் ஆ போல்). Thinaimalai 138: in this boy's father's town the buffalo's milk runs as she thinks of her calf.
links.teaches: Kalittokai 81 gives the cow's pull to its calf to the mother as an open simile, while Thinaimalai 138 leaves the same yearning beast unglossed in the father's own fields, so the pair shows how the marutham poets could turn one image of parental pull from praise of the mother into a silent reproach of the father.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 43: the woman tells the man of the rich town that his bard is a greater liar than he and swears many oaths (பாணன் பொய்யன் பல்சூ ளினனே). Thinaimalai 131: she tells the bard, whose lute is bent like a prawn, not to fashion words of reconciliation, since she has heard the man's lies (ஊரன்பொய்).
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru 43 ranks the bard's lying above the man's in a single comparison, while Thinaimalai 131 dates her refusal from the day she heard the man's own lie and so sets the bard's words aside as useless rather than worse, which shows the go-between's credit in marutham falling with his master's and not on its own.

links.note: Kural 801 defines old friendship (பழைமை) as friendship that does not cut down the liberties of intimacy (கிழமை). Thinaimalai 134 uses both words (கிழமை, பழமை) as two alternative reasons why she, the humble one, received the man's grace when the many women he took did not.
links.teaches: The Kural states as a definition that old intimacy survives the liberties a friend takes, while the wife applies the same two terms to a husband who has taken many women and cannot decide whether his return came from enduring character or from reckoning the use of old ties, so the pair shows the friendship ethic carried into marriage and the doubt it leaves when the one taking liberties is the stronger party.

source_issues: 124-139: the colophon gives only the thinai (மருதம்) and no thurai; every thurai_akam speech situation is inferred from the poem, with occasion words null.
127 line 3: the bracket in என்(று(அணுகான் is misprinted (read என்று அணுகான்), and குலம்காரம் is obscure; the verse is marked uncertain.
130 line 1: என்செய் திரம்நின் றவரை is split oddly and hard to construe; the reading is a guess.
132 lines 3-4: the sense of இறவாது and பின்னாரில் அந்தி முடிவு is unclear.
135: the printed number 35 is a misprint for 135 (flag), and the site lacks this verse; lines 3-4 are hard to construe.
136 line 1: the site's text lacks this line; பண்மகனே may be a misprint for பாண்மகனே; lines 3-4 are obscure.
138 line 1: the site's text lacks this line; வன்றுள்ளி is read as வன் துள்ளி, 'spurting hard'.
139 line 3: தாராத்தோ(று) ஆய்ந்தெடுப்பும் is obscure; the reading takes it as herons picking along the field.
